en: Saṁyutta Nikāya 17.1 (SN 17.1, PTS SN ii 225) 1.
First Chapter: The Dreadful Discourse (Dāruṇasutta)
Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“Monks,” [the Blessed One said]. “Venerable sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One spoke as follows:
“Monks, gain, honor, and fame are harsh, bitter, and cruel, and they are an obstacle to the attainment of the unsurpassed security from bondage.
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus:
‘We will abandon gain, honor, and fame when they arise; and gain, honor, and fame that have arisen shall not take possession of our minds.’”
"In this way, monks, you should train yourselves. Thus was the first [discourse].
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 17.2. (SN 17.2, PTS SN ii 226)
1. First Chapter:
The Hook Discourse.
At Sāvatthī, [the Blessed One] was dwelling.
“Monks, gain, honor, and fame are dreadful, bitter, harsh, and an obstacle to the attainment of the unsurpassed security from bondage.
It is just as if, monks, a fisherman were to cast a baited hook into a deep pool of water,
and a fish, eyeing the bait, were to swallow it.”
"In this way, monks, that fish which has swallowed the hook has fallen into misfortune, has fallen into calamity, and is at the fisherman's disposal to do with as he pleases.
'Fisherman,' monks, is a designation for Māra the Evil One.
'Hook,' monks, is a designation for gain, honor, and fame."
"Monks, whatever monk relishes and desires gain, honor, and fame that have arisen—this monk, monks, is said to be one who has swallowed the bait of Māra;
he has fallen into misfortune, he has fallen into ruin, and he is subject to the doing as he wishes by the Evil One.
So terrible, monks, is gain, honor, and fame: they are bitter, harsh, and an obstacle to the attainment of the unsurpassed security from bondage."
"Therefore, bhikkhus, you should train yourselves thus:
'We will abandon gain, honor, and fame when they arise, and so that gain, honor, and fame which have arisen will not overwhelm our minds.
It is in this way, bhikkhus, that you should train yourselves."
The Second.
Saṃyutta Nikāya 17.3 (SN 17.3, PTS SN ii 226) 1.
First Chapter
The Turtle Discourse.
At Sāvatthī, the Blessed One was staying.
“Monks, gain, honor, and fame are dreadful … [as before] … for the attainment of the unsurpassed security from bondage.”
“Once upon a time, monks, there was a great family of turtles that had lived for a long time in a certain lake.
Then, monks, one turtle said to another turtle:
‘Dear turtle, do not go to that place.’”
Then, monks, that tortoise came to that place.
The hunter pierced it with a trap.
Thereupon, monks, that tortoise approached the other tortoise.
Monks, that turtle saw the other turtle coming from afar.
Having seen him, he said this to the other turtle:
“I hope, dear turtle, that you have not gone to that place?”
“I have indeed come to that place, dear tortoise.
“But I hope, dear tortoise, that you are unhurt and uninjured?
“I am unhurt, dear tortoise, and uninjured; moreover, this cord is following right behind my back.”
“Truly you have been struck down, dear tortoise; truly you have been ruined.
For it was because of this string, dear tortoise, that your father and grandfather met with misfortune and disaster.
Now go away, dear tortoise; you no longer belong to us.”
"Luddo," monks, is a designation for Māra the Evil One.
"Papatā," monks, is a designation for gain, honor, and renown.
"Suttaka," monks, is a designation for delight and lust.
“Monks, whatever monk relishes and desires gain, honor, and praise that has arisen—this monk, monks, is called one who is greedy for a precipice;
he has fallen into misfortune, he has fallen into calamity, and he is at the disposal of the Evil One as he wishes.
Indeed, monks, gain, honor, and praise are so terrible…”
“In this way, bhikkhus, you should train yourselves.
The third [discourse]. Saṁyutta Nikāya 17.4 (SN 17.4, PTS SN ii 228)
1. First Chapter: The Discourse on Long-Haired Horses.
At Sāvatthī, [the Blessed One] was dwelling.
“Bhikkhus, gain, honor, and fame are terrible … for the attainment [of the goal].
Just as if, bhikkhus, a long-haired ewe were to enter a thicket of thorns:
it would get caught here and there, snagged here and there, entangled here and there, and meet with misfortune and disaster here and there.

In the same way, monks, here a certain monk, overcome by gain, honor, and fame, his mind consumed by them, puts on his lower robe in the morning and, taking bowl and robes, enters a village or town for alms. There, in this or that place, he clings;
there, in this or that place, he is gripped; there, in this or that place, he is bound; there, in this or that place, he meets with ruin and disaster.
So terrible, monks, is gain, honor, and fame... [and so on].
“In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
The fourth [discourse].
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 17.5 (SN 17.5, PTS SN ii 228)
1. First Chapter: The Discourse on the Jackal.
[The Blessed One] was dwelling at Sāvatthī.
“Bhikkhus, gain, honor, and fame are terrible... for the attainment [of the goal].
Suppose, bhikkhus, there were a female lizard that was full of dung, filled with dung, and before her was a great heap of dung.
She would despise another female lizard, thinking:”
‘I am like a cesspit, full of excrement and filled with excrement, and before me lies a great heap of excrement.
In the same way, monks, here a certain bhikkhu, overcome and his mind consumed by gain, honor, and fame, dresses in the morning and, taking bowl and robe, enters a village or town for alms.
There he eats as much as he needs, is invited for the following day’s meal, and his bowl is full.
Having gone to the monastery, he boasts in the midst of the community of monks:
"I have eaten my fill; I have been invited for tomorrow's meal; this alms-food of mine is abundant;
I am a recipient of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick; but as for these others..."
‘The monks have little merit and little influence; they do not obtain robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
Overcome by that gain, honor, and fame, his mind consumed by it, he looks down upon other virtuous monks.
For that, monks, leads to the long-term harm and suffering of that foolish man.
"So dreadful, monks, is gain, honor, and fame...
[as before] ...Thus, monks, should you train yourselves.
The fifth.

Saṃyutta Nikāya 17.6 (SN 17.6, PTS SN ii 229) 1. First Chapter: The Chapter on the World The Discourse on the Thunderbolt At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, suppose there were a mountain of rock, a single solid mass of stone, eight thousand leagues in length, breadth, and height, and it would rain down upon it for twenty thousand years. What do you think, bhikkhus? Would that mountain of rock, that single solid mass of stone, be worn away and eliminated by that rain? “It would, Bhante. “Bhikkhus, this great earth is more lasting than that mountain of rock, that single solid mass of stone. Yet, even this great earth will be worn away and eliminated by the aeons. How much more so, then, this body! Therefore, bhikkhus, you should train yourselves thus: ‘We shall be mindful and clearly comprehending while walking; we shall be mindful and clearly comprehending while standing; we shall be mindful and clearly comprehending while sitting; we shall be mindful and clearly comprehending while lying down; we shall be mindful and clearly comprehending while waking. Thus, bhikkhus, should you train yourselves.”
At Sāvatthī, the Blessed One was staying.
“Bhikkhus, gain, honor, and fame are cruel... [as before] ...for the attainment of the unsurpassed security from bondage.
Bhikkhus, whom should a thunderbolt strike? Let gain, honor, and fame fall upon the trainee who has not yet attained his goal.”
“‘The wheel of the thunderbolt,’ monks, is a designation for gain, honor, and renown.
So terrible, monks, is gain, honor, and renown...
Thus, monks, you should train yourselves.”
The Sixth.
Saṃyutta Nikāya 17.7 (SN 17.7, PTS SN ii 229) 1.
First Chapter
The Diddha Sutta.
At Sāvatthī, the Blessed One was staying.
“Monks, gain, honor, and fame are dreadful … [as before] … for the attainment of the unsurpassed security from bondage.”
“Monks, whom should one pierce with a poisoned arrow that has been smeared? One should pierce a trainee who has not yet attained his goal, so that gain, honor, and praise may come upon him.
‘Arrow,’ monks, is a designation for gain, honor, and praise.
So dreadful, monks, is gain, honor, and praise…” [and so on].
“In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
This is the seventh [discourse]. *Saṃyutta Nikāya* 17.8 (SN 17.8, PTS SN ii 230)
1. First Chapter: The Discourse on the Jackal.
[The Blessed One] was dwelling at Sāvatthī.
“Monks, gain, honor, and fame are terrible... [they lead] to the non-attainment of the unattained.
Have you not heard, monks, the cry of a jackal howling at the break of dawn?
“Yes, venerable sir.”
“Monks, that old jackal, afflicted by the disease called *ukkaṇḍaka*, found no pleasure whether he went to his den, or to the foot of a tree, or to the open air;
wherever he went, wherever he stood, wherever he sat, or wherever he lay down, there he met with misfortune and ruin.”

In the same way, monks, here a certain monk, overcome and obsessed by gain, honor, and fame, finds no delight when he has gone to an empty dwelling, finds no delight at the foot of a tree, and finds no delight in the open air;
wherever he goes, wherever he stands, wherever he sits, and wherever he lies down, there he encounters misfortune and ruin.
So dreadful, monks, is gain, honor, and fame... [and so on].
"In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
The eighth.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 17.9 (SN 17.9, PTS SN ii 231).
1. First Chapter: The Discourse on the Veramba Wind.
At Sāvatthī, [the Blessed One] was dwelling.
“Monks, gain, honor, and fame are terrible … [as previously described] … for the attainment of the higher goal.
Monks, in the upper sky there blow winds called the Verambhas.
There, whatever bird goes along is tossed about by those Verambha winds.”
When he is tossed about by the Veramba winds, his feet go in one direction, his wings go in another, his head goes in another,
and his body goes in yet another. In the same way, monks, here a certain bhikkhu, his mind overcome and overwhelmed by gain,
honor, and fame, dresses in the morning and, taking bowl and robe, enters a village or town for alms.
With body unguarded, speech unguarded, mind unguarded, with mindfulness unestablished,
and with the sense faculties unrestrained,
he sees there a woman poorly dressed or poorly clad.
Seeing a woman poorly dressed or poorly clad, lust overcomes his mind.
With a mind overcome by lust, he renounces the training and returns to the lower life.
Others take away his robe, others take away his bowl, others take away his sitting mat, and others take away his needle-case, like a bird carried off by a whirlwind.
"So dreadful, bhikkhus, are gain, honor, and fame...
[as before] ...Thus, bhikkhus, should you train yourselves.
The ninth [sutta].

Saṃyutta Nikāya 17.10 (SN 17.10, PTS SN ii 231) 1. First Chapter: Sagāthakasutta (Verses) “Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who is intent on his own welfare but not on the welfare of others; the person who is intent on the welfare of others but not on his own welfare; the person who is intent neither on his own welfare nor on the welfare of others; and the person who is intent both on his own welfare and on the welfare of others. These, bhikkhus, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. [The Buddha then spoke these verses: “One who is intent on his own welfare, But not on the welfare of others— Such a person is called ‘selfish’ By those who understand the Dhamma. One who is intent on the welfare of others, But not on his own welfare— Such a person is called ‘one who seeks the good of others’ By those who understand the Dhamma. One who is intent neither on his own welfare Nor on the welfare of others— Such a person is called ‘one who harms both himself and others’ By those who understand the Dhamma. One who is intent both on his own welfare And on the welfare of others— Such a person is called ‘one who benefits both himself and others’ By those who understand the Dhamma. “These, bhikkhus, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. [The Buddha then spoke these verses: “The one who is intent on his own welfare And not on the welfare of others— Though he may be intent on his own welfare, He does not reach the ultimate goal. The one who is intent on the welfare of others And not on his own welfare— Though he may be intent on the welfare of others, He does not reach the ultimate goal. The one who is intent neither on his own welfare Nor on the welfare of others— Having harmed both himself and others, He reaches the lowest state. The one who is intent both on his own welfare And on the welfare of others— Having benefited both himself and others, He reaches the highest state. “These, bhikkhus, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. [The Buddha then spoke these verses: “The one who is intent on his own welfare And not on the welfare of others— This person is called ‘the giver of self’ By those who understand the Dhamma. The one who is intent on the welfare of others And not on his own welfare— This person is called ‘the giver of all’ By those who understand the Dhamma. The one who is intent neither on his own welfare Nor on the welfare of others— This person is called ‘the destroyer of both’ By those who understand the Dhamma. The one who is intent both on his own welfare And on the welfare of others— This person is called ‘the giver of both’ By those who understand the Dhamma. “These, bhikkhus, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. [The Buddha then spoke these verses: “The one who is intent on his own welfare And not on the welfare of others— Though he may be intent on his own welfare, He does not reach the ultimate goal. The one who is intent on the welfare of others And not on his own welfare— Though he may be intent on the welfare of others, He does not reach the ultimate goal. The one who is intent neither on his own welfare Nor on the welfare of others— Having harmed both himself and others, He reaches the lowest state. The one who is intent both on his own welfare And on the welfare of others— Having benefited both himself and others, He reaches the highest state. “These, bhikkhus, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. [The Buddha then spoke these verses: “The one who is intent on his own welfare And not on the welfare of others— This person is called ‘one who has crossed over for himself’ By those who understand the Dhamma. The one who is intent on the welfare of others And not on his own welfare— This person is called ‘one who has crossed over for others’ By those who understand the Dhamma. The one who is intent neither on his own welfare Nor on the welfare of others— This person is called ‘one who has not crossed over’ By those who understand the Dhamma. The one who is intent both on his own welfare And on the welfare of others— This person is called ‘one who has crossed over both’ By those who understand the Dhamma.

“These, bhikkhus, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. [The Buddha then spoke these verses: “The one who is intent on his own welfare And not on the welfare of others— Though he may be intent on his own welfare, He does not reach the ultimate goal. The one who is intent on the welfare of others And not on his own welfare— Though he may be intent on the welfare of others, He does not reach the ultimate goal. The one who is intent neither on his own welfare Nor on the welfare of others— Having harmed both himself and others, He reaches the lowest state. The one who is intent both on his own welfare And on the welfare of others— Having benefited both himself and others, He reaches the highest state. “These, bhikkhus, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. [The Buddha then spoke these verses: “The one who is intent on his own welfare And not on the welfare of others— This person is called ‘a disciple’ By those who understand the Dhamma. The one who is intent on the welfare of others And not on his own welfare— This person is called ‘a teacher’ By those who understand the Dhamma. The one who is intent neither on his own welfare Nor on the welfare of others— This person is called ‘neither disciple nor teacher’ By those who understand the Dhamma. The one who is intent both on his own welfare And on the welfare of others— This person is called ‘both disciple and teacher’ By those who understand the Dhamma. “These, bhikkhus, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. [The Buddha then spoke these verses: “The one who is intent on his own welfare And not on the welfare of others— Though he may be intent on his own welfare, He does not reach the ultimate goal. The one who is intent on the welfare of others And not on his own welfare— Though he may be intent on the welfare of others, He does not reach the ultimate goal. The one who is intent neither on his own welfare Nor on the welfare of others— Having harmed both himself and others, He reaches the lowest state. The one who is intent both on his own welfare And on the welfare of others— Having benefited both himself and others, He reaches the highest state. “These, bhikkhus, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. [The Buddha then spoke these verses: “The one who is intent on his own welfare And not on the welfare of others— This person is called ‘one who has entered the stream’ By those who understand the Dhamma. The one who is intent on the welfare of others And not on his own welfare— This person is called ‘one who has reached the further shore’ By those who understand the Dhamma. The one who is intent neither on his own welfare Nor on the welfare of others— This person is called ‘one who has not entered the stream’ By those who understand the Dhamma. The one who is intent both on his own welfare And on the welfare of others— This person is called ‘one who has reached the further shore of both’ By those who understand the Dhamma. “These, bhikkhus, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. [The Buddha then spoke these verses: “The one who is intent on his own welfare And not on the welfare of others— Though he may be intent on his own welfare, He does not reach the ultimate goal. The one who is intent on the welfare of others And not on his own welfare— Though he may be intent on the welfare of others, He does not reach the ultimate goal. The one who is intent neither on his own welfare Nor on the welfare of others— Having harmed both himself and others, He reaches the lowest state. The one who is intent both on his own welfare And on the welfare of others— Having benefited both himself and others, He reaches the highest state. “These, bhikkhus, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. [The Buddha then spoke these verses: “The one who is intent on his own welfare And not on the welfare of others— This person is called ‘one who has attained Nibbāna for himself
At Sāvatthī. "Bhikkhus, gain, honor, and fame are harsh... [as before] ...for the attainment of the unsurpassed security from bondage.

Here, bhikkhus, I see a certain person who, being overcome by honor and with a mind consumed by it, is reborn, with the breakup of the body after death, in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, the lower world, hell.

“Furthermore, monks, here I see a certain person who, overcome by lack of honor and with mind obsessed by it, is reborn after the breakup of the body, after death, in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm,
hell. Furthermore, monks, here I see a certain person who, overcome by both honor and lack of honor,
and with mind obsessed by both, is reborn after the breakup of the body, after death, in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, hell.”
“Monks, gain, honor, and fame are indeed so terrible...
[as before] ...Thus, monks, you should train yourselves.
This is what the Blessed One said.
Having said this, the Sugata, the Teacher, then further spoke these words:
“For one who is being honored, or for one who is not honored— both cases alike;”
The concentration of one who dwells in the immeasurables does not waver;
that meditator is constant.
Subtle, possessing insight into views,
delighting in the destruction of clinging—
such a one they call a true person.
The tenth.
The first chapter.
Its summary verse:
The terrible fishhook, the tortoise,
the long-haired porpoise,
the lightning-bolt, and the jackal.
*Verambha-saṃyutta with Verses*.
Saṃyutta Nikāya 17.11 (SN 17.11, PTS SN ii 233).
Chapter 2. Second Section.
The Discourse on the Golden Bowl.
At Sāvatthī, the Blessed One was staying there.
“Monks, gain, honor, and fame are harsh... [and so on] ...for the attainment of the unsurpassed security from bondage.”
In this case, monks, having encompassed the mind of a certain person with my own mind, I understand:
"This venerable one would not speak a deliberate lie even for the sake of a bowl filled with gold dust.
Yet, at a later time, I see him speaking a deliberate lie, his mind overcome and consumed by gain, honor, and fame.
"So terrible, bhikkhus, are gain, honor, and fame...
[as before] ...Thus, bhikkhus, should you train yourselves.
The first.

Saṁyutta Nikāya 17.12 (SN 17.12, PTS SN ii 233) 2. Second Chapter: The Silver Bowl Discourse “Bhikkhus, suppose there were a silver bowl, polished, bright, highly refined, and translucent. Whatever food or drink were placed into it would appear as its own color. So too, bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu is thus liberated in mind, whatever feeling he feels—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—he understands it as it really is: ‘This is a feeling that is subject to arising; this is a feeling that is subject to vanishing; this is a feeling that is subject to alteration. When he knows and sees thus, his mind inclines toward revulsion toward all feelings. Through revulsion, his mind becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion, he is liberated. When liberated, there comes the knowledge: ‘It is liberated. He understands: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being.’”
Staying at Sāvatthī:
“Bhikkhus, gain, honor, and fame are harsh… Here, bhikkhus,
having encompassed the mind with my own mind, I understand a certain person thus:”
‘This venerable one would not knowingly speak a falsehood even for the sake of a bowl full of gold dust.
Yet at a later time, I see him overcome and his mind consumed by gain, honor, and fame, speaking a falsehood knowingly.
So terrible, monks, is gain, honor, and fame... [as before]...
“In this way, bhikkhus, you should train yourselves.
The second [sutta].
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 17.13–20 (SN 17.13, PTS SN ii 233).
2. The Second Chapter:
The Group of Eight on the Golden Coin, etc.
[The Blessed One] was dwelling at Sāvatthī.
“Here, monks, having encompassed the mind with my own mind, I understand a certain person thus:
‘This venerable one would not, for the sake of even a single gold coin...
nor for the sake of a hundred gold coins...’”
For the sake of even a single piece of gold,
for the sake of even a hundred pieces of gold,
and for the sake of even the earth filled with gold...
‘One might speak a deliberate lie even for the sake of some trifling material gain… even for the sake of one’s life… or even for the sake of Janapadakalyāṇī.’”
But on another occasion, I see him overcome by gain, honor, and fame, his mind consumed, speaking deliberate falsehoods.
So terrible indeed, monks, is gain, honor, and fame...
Thus, monks, you should train yourselves.”
The tenth.
The second chapter.
Its summary verse:
Two bowls and two golden ones,
and two others made of jasper;
the earth, some trifle, and my life—
The Ten [Qualities] of Janapadakalyāṇī.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 17.21 (SN 17.21, PTS SN ii 234) 3.
Third Chapter.
The Discourse on Women.
At Sāvatthī, the Blessed One was staying there.
“Bhikkhus, gain, honor, and fame are dreadful … [as before] …”
“Monks, women do not remain obsessing the mind of one whose mind remains obsessed by gain, honor, and fame.
Indeed, monks, gain, honor, and fame are so dreadful...
Thus, monks, you should train yourselves.”
First.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 17.22 (SN 17.22, PTS SN ii 235) 3.
Third Chapter (Tatiyavagga)
The Kalyāṇī Sutta. At Sāvatthī.
“Monks, gain, honor, and fame are dreadful … [as before] …”
“Monks, the most beautiful woman in the land does not obsess the mind of one whose mind is obsessed by gain, honor, and fame.
So terrible, monks, is gain, honor, and fame...
Thus, monks, you should train yourselves.”
The Second.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 17.23 (SN 17.23, PTS SN ii 235) 3.
Third Chapter (Tatiyavagga)
The Discourse on the Only Son.
At Sāvatthī, the Blessed One was staying there. “Bhikkhus, gain, honor, and renown are cruel... [as before] ...”
“Bhikkhus, a female lay follower endowed with faith might rightly entreat her only son, who is dear and beloved, saying:
‘Dear one, may you become like Citta the householder and Hatthaka of Āḷavī.
Bhikkhus, this is the standard, this is the measure for my male lay disciples, namely Citta the householder and Hatthaka of Āḷavī.”
"If you, dear son, go forth from the home life into homelessness,
then be like Sāriputta and Moggallāna.
Monks, this is the standard, this is the measure for my monk-disciples, namely Sāriputta and Moggallāna.
"And yet, dear one, may gain, honor, and praise not come upon you while you are still a trainee who has not yet attained his goal.
Monks, if gain, honor, and praise come upon that monk who is still a trainee and has not yet attained his goal, it becomes an obstacle for him.
So terrible, monks, is gain, honor, and praise... [as before]...
"In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
The third [sutta].
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 17.24. (SN 17.24, PTS SN ii 236)
3. The Third Chapter: The Discourse on the Single Daughter.
At Sāvatthī, [the Blessed One] was dwelling.
“Monks, gain, honor, and fame are terrible...
Monks, a female lay follower with faith, when making a proper request for her one daughter who is dear and pleasing, would request thus:
‘Noble lady, may you become like the female lay follower Khujjuttarā and Veḷukaṇḍakīyā Nandamātā.’”
“Monks, this is the scale, this is the measure for my female lay disciples: namely, the lay disciple Khujjuttarā and Veḷukaṇḍakiyā Nandamātā.
If you, noble lady, go forth from the home life into homelessness, then become like the bhikkhunīs Khemā and Uppalavaṇṇā.”
“Monks, this is the standard, this is the measure for my female disciples among the bhikkhunīs, namely the bhikkhunīs Khemā and Uppalavaṇṇā.
But, noble lady, may gain, honor, and fame not come upon you while you are still a trainee who has not yet attained her goal.
Monks, if gain, honor, and fame should come upon that bhikkhunī who is still a trainee who has not yet attained her goal, it becomes an obstacle for her.”
“Monks, gain, honor, and fame are indeed so dreadful...
[as before] ...Thus, monks, you should train yourselves.
The fourth.

Saṁyutta Nikāya 17.25 (SN 17.25, PTS SN ii 236) 3. Tatiyavagga Samaṇabrāhmaṇasutta “Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of ascetics and brahmins to be found existing in the world. What four? The one who is a mere renouncer; the one who lives by the rules of purification; the one who is a tormentor; and the one who has attained final knowledge. And how, bhikkhus, is one an ascetic who is a mere renouncer? Here, bhikkhus, some ascetic or brahmin, having shaved off his hair and beard, gone forth from the home life into homelessness, and being clothed in robes made of rags, does not abstain from taking what is not given, unchastity, false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, idle chatter, covetousness, ill will, and wrong view. He does not abstain from these ten courses of unwholesome action. This, bhikkhus, is called an ascetic who is a mere renouncer. And how, bhikkhus, is one an ascetic who lives by the rules of purification? Here, bhikkhus, some ascetic or brahmin, having shaved off his hair and beard... [as above] ...does not abstain from these ten courses of unwholesome action, yet he observes various rules of purification such as: ‘I shall not wear clothes from a village,’ or ‘I shall wear clothes from a charnel ground,’ or ‘I shall wear clothes made of grass,’ or ‘I shall wear clothes made of bark,’ or ‘I shall wear clothes made of wood-shavings,’ or ‘I shall wear clothes made of owls’ wings,’ or ‘I shall go naked. He observes such rules of purification. This, bhikkhus, is called an ascetic who lives by the rules of purification. And how, bhikkhus, is one an ascetic who is a tormentor? Here, bhikkhus, some ascetic or brahmin, having shaved off his hair and beard... [as above] ...does not abstain from these ten courses of unwholesome action, yet he torments himself with various mortifications:

he stands on one foot, he dwells in the fire’s heat, he lies on a bed of thorns, he drinks only hot water, he eats only once a day, he eats only at every fourth mealtime, or he follows other such painful practices. This, bhikkhus, is called an ascetic who is a tormentor. And how, bhikkhus, is one an ascetic who has attained final knowledge? Here, bhikkhus, some ascetic or brahmin, having shaved off his hair and beard, gone forth from the home life into homelessness, and being clothed in robes made of rags, abstains from taking what is not given, unchastity, false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, idle chatter, covetousness, ill will, and wrong view. He abstains from these ten courses of unwholesome action. Having abandoned these ten courses of unwholesome action, he develops the ten wholesome courses of action. He develops the mind of loving-kindness toward one quarter, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth; thus above, below, across, and everywhere, to all as to himself, he dwells pervading the entire world with a mind of loving-kindness—vast, exalted, immeasurable, without hostility, and without ill will. He develops the mind of compassion... the mind of sympathetic joy... the mind of equanimity toward one quarter... [as above]. This, bhikkhus, is called an ascetic who has attained final knowledge. These, bhikkhus, are the four kinds of ascetics and brahmins to be found existing in the world.”

Staying at Sāvatthī, [the Blessed One said]: “Bhikkhus, whatever ascetics or brahmins do not understand, as they really are, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding gain, honor, and renown— they, bhikkhus,
are not ascetics among ascetics, nor are they brahmins among brahmins.”

They are esteemed by the brahmins, yet those venerable ones do not dwell having personally realized, through direct knowledge, and attained in this very life, the goal of asceticism or the goal of brahminhood.
But whatever recluses or brahmins, monks, understand as they really are the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding gain, honor, and fame—
"And those recluses or brahmins, monks, who are esteemed as recluses among recluses and as brahmins among brahmins— they, those venerable ones,
having realized for themselves through direct knowledge in this very life the goal of the recluse and the goal of the brahmin, enter upon and abide in it."
The Fifth.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 17.26 (SN 17.26, PTS SN ii 237) 3.
Third Chapter (Tatiyavagga)
The Second Discourse on Ascetics and Brahmins. At Sāvatthī.

“Bhikkhus, whatever ascetics or brahmins do not understand, as they really are, the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding gain, honor, and renown... [as before] ...”
“They understand … [and so on] … having realized it for themselves through direct knowledge, they enter and dwell therein.
The sixth.

Saṁyutta Nikāya 17.27 (SN 17.27, PTS SN ii 237) 3. Third Chapter The Discourse on Ascetics and Brahmins (Third) “Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of ascetics and brahmins to be found existing in the world. What four? “The one who is like a raft; the one who is like a bath; the one who is like a lotus; and the one who has crossed over and gone beyond. “And how, bhikkhus, is an ascetic or brahmin ‘one who is like a raft’? Here, bhikkhus, an ascetic or brahmin has not abandoned lust, hatred, and delusion; he has not removed them from within himself. Yet he instructs others: ‘Abandon lust, hatred, and delusion! Remove them from yourselves! “Just as a man in need of a raft, seeking a raft, wandering in search of a raft, might construct a raft from grass, wood, reeds, and bamboo, and by means of that raft cross over from this shore to the far shore—so too, bhikkhus, when an ascetic or brahmin has not abandoned lust, hatred, and delusion, yet instructs others to abandon them, he is called an ascetic or brahmin ‘one who is like a raft. “And how, bhikkhus, is an ascetic or brahmin ‘one who is like a bath’? Here, bhikkhus, an ascetic or brahmin has not abandoned lust, hatred, and delusion; he has not removed them from within himself. Yet he instructs others: ‘Bathe! Purify yourselves! “Just as a man who is dirty, soiled, and covered in mud might go to a bathing place, enter the water, and bathe and wash away the dirt and filth—so too, bhikkhus, when an ascetic or brahmin has not abandoned lust, hatred, and delusion, yet instructs others to bathe and purify themselves, he is called an ascetic or brahmin ‘one who is like a bath. “And how, bhikkhus, is an ascetic or brahmin ‘one who is like a lotus’? Here, bhikkhus, an ascetic or brahmin has not abandoned lust, hatred, and delusion; he has not removed them from within himself. Yet he instructs others: ‘Be pure like a lotus! “Just as a blue, red, or white lotus, though born in the water and grown in the water, rises up above the water and remains unsullied by it—so too, bhikkhus, when an ascetic or brahmin has not abandoned lust, hatred, and delusion, yet instructs others to be pure like a lotus, he is called an ascetic or brahmin ‘one who is like a lotus. “And how, bhikkhus, is an ascetic or brahmin ‘one who has crossed over and gone beyond’? Here, bhikkhus, an ascetic or brahmin has abandoned lust, hatred, and delusion; he has removed them from within himself. He does not instruct others to abandon them, nor does he instruct them to bathe, nor does he instruct them to be pure like a lotus. “Just as a man who has crossed over and gone beyond would not instruct those still on this shore to cross over, nor would he instruct them to bathe, nor would he instruct them to be pure like a lotus—so too, bhikkhus, when an ascetic or brahmin has abandoned lust, hatred, and delusion, and does not instruct others in such ways, he is called an ascetic or brahmin ‘one who has crossed over and gone beyond. “These, bhikkhus, are the four kinds of ascetics and brahmins to be found existing in the world.”
Staying at Sāvatthī:
“Bhikkhus, whatever ascetics or brahmins do not understand gain, honor, and renown as they really are;
do not understand the origin of gain, honor, and renown; do not understand the cessation of gain, honor, and renown;”
“They do not understand the practice leading to the cessation of gain, honor,
and fame … [as before] … they understand it … [as before] … having realized it for themselves through direct knowledge, they enter upon and abide in it.”
Seventh.
Saṃyutta Nikāya 17.28 (SN 17.28, PTS SN ii 237) 3.
Third Chapter (Tatiyavagga)
The Chavisutta: At Sāvatthī.
“Monks, gain, honor, and fame are dreadful.”
Gain, honor, and renown, monks, cut through the outer skin; having cut through the outer skin, they cut through the inner skin; having cut through the inner skin, they cut through the flesh;
having cut through the flesh, they cut through the tendons; having cut through the tendons, they cut through the bones;
and having cut through the bones, they remain striking against the marrow.
"So dreadful, bhikkhus, are gain, honor, and fame...
Thus, bhikkhus, should you train yourselves.
The eighth.

Saṃyutta Nikāya 17.29 (SN 17.29, PTS SN ii 238) 3. Third Chapter: The Chapter on the Rope (Tatiyavagga) The Discourse on the Rope (Rajjusutta) “Monks, suppose there were a man who, having entered a dense forest, saw a rope coiled up on the ground. Seeing it, he would think: ‘This is not a snake; this is a rope. Having seen it as it really is with right wisdom, his fear of the snake would vanish. In the same way, monks, when a noble disciple sees the eye as it really is with right wisdom—its origin, its passing away, its gratification, its danger, and the escape from it—then, seeing it thus, he becomes disenchanted with the eye. He becomes disenchanted with the ear... the nose... the tongue... the body... the mind. Being disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion, he is liberated. Through liberation, there is the knowledge: ‘It is liberated. He understands: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being.’”
At Sāvatthī. "Monks, gain, honor, and fame are dreadful.
Gain, honor, and fame, monks, cut through the outer skin; having cut through the outer skin, they cut through the inner skin."
Having cut through the flesh, it cuts through the muscle; having cut through the muscle, it cuts through the sinew; having cut through the sinew, it cuts through the bone;
and having cut through the bone, it remains striking against the marrow.
It is just as if, monks, a strong man were to wrap a stout hair-rope around a calf and rub it.
It would cut through the outer skin; having cut through the outer skin, it would cut through the inner skin; having cut through the inner skin, it would cut through the flesh;

having cut through the flesh, it would cut through the sinews; having cut through the sinews, it would cut through the bone; and having cut through the bone, it would stand reaching right to the marrow.
In the same way, monks, gain, honor, and fame cut through the outer skin; having cut through the outer skin, they cut through the inner skin... [and so on].
It cuts; having cut through the skin, it cuts through the flesh; having cut through the flesh, it cuts through the sinews;
having cut through the sinews, it cuts through the bone; having cut through the bone, it remains striking against the marrow.
So terrible, monks, is gain, honor, and fame... [as above]...
“In this way, bhikkhus, you should train yourselves.
The ninth [sutta].
Saṁyutta Nikāya 17.30 (SN 17.30, PTS SN ii 238)
3. Third Chapter:
The Discourse on Monks.
At Sāvatthī, he was staying.
“Bhikkhus, even for a bhikkhu who is an arahant, one whose taints are destroyed, I say that gain, honor, and praise are an obstacle.
When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One:
“But why, Bhante, would gain, honor, and praise be an obstacle for a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed?”
“Ānanda, as for that unshakable liberation of mind, I do not say that gain, honor, and fame are an obstacle to its attainment.
But, Ānanda, regarding those pleasant dwellings in this very life that are attained by one who dwells diligent, ardent, and resolute—I do say that gain, honor, and fame are an obstacle to these.
Indeed, Ānanda, gain, honor, and fame are so dreadful, bitter, harsh, and obstructive to the attainment of the unsurpassed security from bondage.”
"Therefore, Ānanda, you should train yourselves thus:
‘We will abandon gain, honor, and fame when they arise, and gain, honor, and fame that have arisen shall not obsess our minds.
In this way, Ānanda, you should train yourselves.”
The tenth.
The third chapter.
Its summary verse:
A virtuous woman,
a son, and an only daughter;
three types of ascetics and brahmins—
"Skin and cord, O bhikkhunī.
Saṃyutta Nikāya 17.31 (SN 17.31,
PTS SN ii 239), Chapter Four.
The Bhindī Sutta.
At Sāvatthī, the Blessed One was staying there.
“Monks, gain, honor, and fame are terrible.”
"Overcome and consumed by gain, honor, and fame, monks, Devadatta split the Saṅgha.
So terrible, monks, is gain, honor, and fame... [as before] ...thus should you train."
First.
Saṃyutta Nikāya 17.32 (SN 17.32, PTS SN ii 240) 4.
The Fourth Chapter
The Discourse on the Roots of Skillfulness. At Sāvatthī.
"Monks, gain, honor, and fame are dreadful."
“Monks, when Devadatta was overcome and his mind consumed by gain, honor, and fame, his roots of merit came to total destruction.
Monks, gain, honor, and fame are indeed so dreadful... [as before] ...thus should you train.”
The Second.
Saṃyutta Nikāya 17.33 (SN 17.33, PTS SN ii 240) 4.
The Fourth Chapter
The Discourse on Wholesome States.
At Sāvatthī, the Blessed One was staying. "Monks, gain, honor, and fame are harsh."
“Bhikkhus, when Devadatta was overcome and his mind possessed by gain, honor, and fame, the wholesome Dhamma perished within him.
So terrible, bhikkhus, is gain, honor, and fame... [as before] ...thus should you train yourselves.”
Third.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 17.34 (SN 17.34, PTS SN ii 240) 4.
Fourth Chapter
The Discourse on Wholesome Qualities. At Sāvatthī.
“Monks, gain, honor, and fame are harsh.”
“Monks, for Devadatta, whose mind was overwhelmed and consumed by gain, honor, and fame, the wholesome quality (dhamma) of purity came to utter destruction.
So terrible, monks, is gain, honor, and fame… [as before] …thus should you train.”
The Fourth.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 17.35 (SN 17.35, PTS SN ii 241) 4.
The Fourth Chapter.
The Discourse on Having Just Departed.
At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha on Vulture Peak Mountain, not long after Devadatta had departed.
There, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus concerning Devadatta:
“Bhikkhus, Devadatta’s gain, honor, and fame arose for his own destruction; Devadatta’s gain, honor, and fame arose for his ruin.

Just as, bhikkhus, the plantain tree gives fruit for its own destruction and gives fruit for its ruin, even so, bhikkhus, Devadatta’s gain, honor, and fame arose for his own destruction; Devadatta’s gain, honor, and fame arose for his ruin.”
Just as, monks, a bamboo tree bears fruit for its own destruction and bears fruit for its ruin;
even so, monks, gain, honor, and fame arose for Devadatta for his own destruction and arose for Devadatta for his ruin.
Just as, monks, a reed bears fruit for its own destruction and bears fruit for its ruin; [so it was with Devadatta].
In the same way, monks, Devadatta’s gain, honor, and fame arose for his own destruction; Devadatta’s gain, honor, and fame arose for his ruin.
Just as, monks, a mule conceives a fetus for her own destruction, conceives a fetus for her ruin;
even so, monks, Devadatta’s gain, honor, and fame arose for his own destruction; Devadatta’s gain, honor, and fame arose for his ruin.
“Monks, gain, honor, and fame are indeed so dreadful.
Thus, monks, you should train yourselves.
This is what the Blessed One said.
Having said this, the Sugata, the Teacher, further spoke these words:
“Indeed, the fruit destroys the plantain;
the fruit destroys the bamboo; the fruit destroys the reed.”
“Honors kill the base man,
just as the fetus kills the mule.
Thus ends the fifth [verse].

Saṃyutta Nikāya 17.36 (SN 17.36, PTS SN ii 242) 4. The Fourth Chapter: The Discourse on the Five Hundred Chariots “Bhikkhus, suppose there were five hundred chariots, all yoked together, traveling along a road. A man would come along from the east, and he would say: ‘I will go where those five hundred chariots are going. Then a second man would come along from the west, and he would say: ‘I will go where those five hundred chariots are going. Then a third man would come along from the north, and he would say: ‘I will go where those five hundred chariots are going. Then a fourth man would come along from the south, and he would say: ‘I will go where those five hundred chariots are going. Now, bhikkhus, what do you think? Would those four men meet with those five hundred chariots? “Yes, venerable sir. “Bhikkhus, so too, when a noble disciple possesses four things, he is one who has arrived at the destination, one who has reached the ultimate end, a brahmin who has completed his task, an arahant whose taints are destroyed. What four? Here, bhikkhus, a noble disciple possesses confirmed confidence in the Buddha thus: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Enlightened One, the Blessed One. He possesses confirmed confidence in the Dhamma thus: ‘The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise. He possesses confirmed confidence in the Saṅgha thus: ‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way, practicing the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals—this Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. He possesses the virtues dear to the noble ones—untorn, unbroken, unspotted, unsplattered, liberating, praised by the wise, untarnished, leading to concentration. Possessing these four things, bhikkhus, a noble disciple is one who has arrived at the destination, one who has reached the ultimate end, a brahmin who has completed his task, an arahant whose taints are destroyed.”
The Blessed One was staying at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
Now at that time, Prince Ajātasattu was going to wait upon Devadatta morning and evening with five hundred chariots, and five hundred servings of food from pots were being brought as an offering.

Then a number of bhikkhus approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, they sat down to one side. As they were sitting there, those bhikkhus said this to the Blessed One:
“Bhante, Prince Ajātasattu goes to wait upon Devadatta morning and evening with five hundred chariots, and five hundred servings of cooked rice are brought as an offering of food.
“Monks, do not envy Devadatta’s gain, honor, and fame.
Monks, for as long as Prince Ajātasattu goes to wait upon Devadatta morning and evening with five hundred chariots...”
"He will go to wait upon him, and five hundred offerings of cooked rice will be brought as alms for him.
But, monks, only a decline in wholesome qualities is to be expected for Devadatta, not growth.
Just as if, monks, one were to break bile into the nose of a fierce dog, that dog would become even more fierce than before."
"In the same way, monks, as long as Prince Ajātasattu goes to attend upon Devadatta morning and evening with five hundred chariots,
and five hundred servings of cooked rice are brought as a meal offering,
only decline, monks, is to be expected for Devadatta in regard to wholesome qualities, not growth."
"So terrible, monks, is gain, honor, and fame...
[as before] ...Thus, monks, you should train yourselves.
The sixth.

Saṁyutta Nikāya 17.37 (SN 17.37, PTS SN ii 242) 4. Catutthavagga Mātusutta “Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who is like a mother, the person who is like a father, the person who is like a brother, and the person who is like a friend and companion. And how, bhikkhus, is one a person like a mother? Here, bhikkhus, whatever kind of advice a person gives, they give it with a mind of loving-kindness, not with a mind of hatred; whatever kind of instruction they give, they give it with a mind of loving-kindness, not with a mind of hatred. Just as a mother would give advice and instruction to her only child with a mind of loving-kindness, not with a mind of hatred, so too, bhikkhus, whatever kind of advice a person gives, they give it with a mind of loving-kindness, not with a mind of hatred; whatever kind of instruction they give, they give it with a mind of loving-kindness, not with a mind of hatred. It is in this way that one is a person like a mother. And how, bhikkhus, is one a person like a father? Here, bhikkhus, whatever kind of advice a person gives, they give it with a mind of harmlessness, not with a mind of cruelty; whatever kind of instruction they give, they give it with a mind of harmlessness, not with a mind of cruelty. Just as a father would give advice and instruction to his only child with a mind of harmlessness, not with a mind of cruelty, so too, bhikkhus, whatever kind of advice a person gives, they give it with a mind of harmlessness, not with a mind of cruelty; whatever kind of instruction they give, they give it with a mind of harmlessness, not with a mind of cruelty. It is in this way that one is a person like a father. And how, bhikkhus, is one a person like a brother? Here, bhikkhus, whatever kind of advice a person gives, they give it with a mind of respect, not with a mind of contempt; whatever kind of instruction they give, they give it with a mind of respect, not with a mind of contempt. Just as a brother would give advice and instruction to a brother with a mind of respect, not with a mind of contempt, so too, bhikkhus, whatever kind of advice a person gives, they give it with a mind of respect, not with a mind of contempt; whatever kind of instruction they give, they give it with a mind of respect, not with a mind of contempt. It is in this way that one is a person like a brother. And how, bhikkhus, is one a person like a friend and companion? Here, bhikkhus, whatever kind of advice a person gives, they give it with a mind of sympathy, not with a mind of hostility; whatever kind of instruction they give, they give it with a mind of sympathy, not with a mind of hostility. Just as a friend or companion would give advice and instruction to a friend or companion with a mind of sympathy, not with a mind of hostility, so too, bhikkhus, whatever kind of advice a person gives, they give it with a mind of sympathy, not with a mind of hostility; whatever kind of instruction they give, they give it with a mind of sympathy, not with a mind of hostility. It is in this way that one is a person like a friend and companion. These, bhikkhus, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world.”
Staying at Sāvatthī:
“Monks, gain, honor, and fame are harsh, bitter, cruel, and an obstacle to the attainment of the unsurpassed security from bondage.
Here, monks, having encompassed the mind with my own mind, I understand a certain person thus:”
‘This venerable one would not intentionally speak a falsehood even for the sake of his mother.
Yet at a later time, I see him, overcome and possessed by gain, honor, and praise, speaking a deliberate lie.
So terrible, monks, is gain, honor, and praise—so bitter, harsh, and an obstacle to the attainment of the unsurpassed security from bondage.
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus:
“We will abandon gain, honor, and fame when they arise;
and gain, honor, and fame that have arisen shall not overwhelm our minds.”
“In this way, bhikkhus, you should train yourselves.
The seventh [sutta].
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 17.38–43 (SN 17.38, PTS SN ii 243).
4. The Fourth Chapter:
The Hexad on the Discourse to the Father, etc.
[The Blessed One] was dwelling at Sāvatthī.
“Monks, gain, honor, and fame are terrible, bitter, harsh, and an obstacle to the attainment of the unsurpassed security from bondage.
Here, monks, having encompassed the mind of a certain person with my own mind, I understand:
‘This venerable one would not even for the sake of his father...’”
(To be expanded in full: ...
for the sake of a brother ...
for the sake of a sister ...
‘For the sake of a son...
for the sake of a daughter...
or for the sake of a wife, one might knowingly speak falsehood.’”
Then, at a later time, I see him overcome by gain, honor, and fame, his mind consumed, speaking deliberate falsehoods.
So terrible, monks, is gain, honor, and fame—bitter, harsh, and an obstacle to the attainment of the unsurpassed security from bondage.
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus:
‘We shall abandon gain, honor, and fame when they arise, and let not the gain, honor, and fame that have arisen obsess our minds.
In this way, monks, you should train yourselves. Thus ends the thirteenth [discourse].
The Fourth Chapter.
Its summary (uddāna) is:
"He split the root; two things."
The chariot has departed for its mother;
[it is followed by] the father, the brother,
the sister, the son, the daughter, and the wife.
The Connected Discourses on Gain and Honor are complete.
